purpose: Exercise different routing patterns in a Mixtral-family MoE without assuming that experts map cleanly to human-readable domains.
design_principles: Do not assume there is a neat math expert, code expert, or legal expert. MoE routing is token-level and can specialize around syntax, language, format, or style as much as topic.
Probe across contrasting token regimes: natural prose, code, SQL, JSON, XML, shell, logs, math notation, markdown tables, and multilingual text.
Keep generation deterministic when possible so routing differences are easier to compare across repeated runs.
Use paired and hybrid prompts so we can test whether routing changes with format alone, with topic alone, or with both together.
recommended_protocol: Run every prompt at least twice with the same generation settings.
Start with the single-format families before the hybrid families.
If expert IDs become visible later, compare both unique experts touched and stable co-activation patterns across repeats.
Treat this suite as a coverage sweep, not a proof that a prompt exclusively belongs to one expert.

families.routing_hypothesis: Long natural-language prose and editorial rewriting may cluster on a stable subset of experts distinct from heavy syntax or code prompts.

messages.content:
Summarize the memo below into exactly four bullets and one one-sentence recommendation.

Memo:
During the last two release cycles, inference latency spiked whenever long prompts arrived while several large background models were still warm in memory. Engineers observed that the worst tail latencies happened after a burst of code-assistant traffic because the system kept the same heavy experts resident even when the next request mostly needed ordinary reasoning. We need a runtime that can decide whether to keep experts warm for reuse or free that memory to preserve longer context.

Abstract:
We evaluated a memory-aware sparse inference policy on a synthetic long-context benchmark. Compared with a fixed-residency baseline, the adaptive policy reduced reload events by 28% at short context lengths while preserving higher context retention on long prompts.
